title: Won't go home
stem:
You are an F2 doctor in orthopaedics. Mr Rowe, 79, had a fractured wrist fixed four days ago and has been declared medically fit for discharge. The physiotherapists and occupational therapists say he is safe to go home, and a care package starts tomorrow.

He refuses to leave, saying he "can't manage" alone, and becomes angry when the nurse mentions his transport.
instruction: Choose the 3 most appropriate actions to take in this situation.

options.text: Call security to escort him to the transport.
options.brief: Escalates a situation that needs listening.
options.detailed: He is anxious, not dangerous. Involving security is disproportionate and distressing.

options.text: Tell him he is preventing another patient from getting a bed.
options.brief: Puts pressure on him rather than addressing his worries.
options.detailed: Bed pressures are real, but this makes him feel guilty without helping him feel safe.

options.text: Keep him in for another week to avoid conflict.
options.brief: Unnecessary hospital stays carry their own risks.
options.detailed: Staying longer than needed increases the risk of deconditioning and infection, and doesn't address his fears.

options.text: Ask his daughter to come and take him home.
options.brief: May help, but it bypasses his concerns.
options.detailed: Family can be part of the solution, but asking her to collect him without understanding his worries may not help.

options.text: Ask him what worries him about going home.
options.brief: His specific fears may be addressable.
options.detailed: He may be worried about meals, stairs, falling or loneliness. Understanding exactly what worries him is the first step to resolving it.

options.text: Ask the therapists to review whether his support is enough.
options.brief: A second look may address his concerns.
options.detailed: If his concerns reveal something missed, such as no one to help in the evenings, the therapists can adjust the plan.

options.text: Tell him the decision has been made and he has to go.
options.brief: Dismissive, and likely to increase his distress.
options.detailed: Discharge decisions are clinical, but delivering one this way ignores his anxiety and may escalate his anger.

options.text: Explain calmly what support is in place for him at home.
options.detailed: He may not know the details of his care package or the follow-up arranged. Explaining them calmly may ease his anxiety.

explanation.issue: This tests how you respond to a patient who refuses discharge because of anxiety, rather than seeing it simply as obstruction.
explanation.keyDetails: He has been assessed as safe. A care package is arranged. He is anxious and angry.
explanation.reasoning: [E] explores his fears, [F] checks the plan, and [H] explains it. The distractors escalate ([A]), pressure him ([B], [G]), avoid the issue ([C]), or bypass him ([D]).
explanation.competing: [D] could be part of the solution, but only once you understand what he is worried about.

references.title: Good medical practice
references.note: Domain 2, listening to patients and responding to their concerns.
